cards.title: Footer text block to offset image-heavy emails
cards.summary: Pad image-heavy campaigns with invisible footer text to reduce spammy image-to-text ratios in Gmail's eyes.
cards.use_when: Before scheduling a design-heavy campaign or hero-image email that contains little body copy, when you want to reduce the risk of promotions/spam placement.

cards.title: Link and alt-text pass before a campaign goes out
cards.summary: Finish every email by wiring all image/button links and writing alt text, then test-send before scheduling.
cards.use_when: Final QA step on any campaign, after copy and design are done and before scheduling the send.

cards.title: Treat deliverability as a sender reputation score
cards.summary: Inbox providers rank you like a credit score: good reputation lands in primary, bad lands in spam, mediocre lands in promotions.
cards.use_when: When diagnosing why campaigns aren't being seen, or when deciding whether low revenue is a content problem or a placement problem.

cards.title: Improve the emails before chasing technical fixes
cards.summary: The source's number-one deliverability lever is simply sending better, more varied, engaging email content.
cards.use_when: When open rates are low and you're tempted to look for technical hacks instead of fixing the content your list receives.

cards.title: Build 14/30/60/90-day engaged segments
cards.summary: Create rolling engagement segments defined by opens or clicks in the last 14, 30, 60 and 90 days, excluding bounces.
cards.use_when: Setting up the segment structure before running a deliverability recovery, or before deciding who should be in your base sending list.

cards.title: Six-week deliverability recovery protocol
cards.summary: Warm reputation back by sending only to tight engaged segments, then expanding as open rates hold.
cards.use_when: When campaigns are landing in spam/promotions and you want a structured plan to regain primary inbox placement.

cards.title: Keep only high-engagement flows during recovery
cards.summary: Pause most automations and lean on welcome, abandon and post-purchase flows, which reliably earn high engagement.
cards.use_when: Deciding which automations to leave running while rebuilding sender reputation, or which flows to prioritize when you can't build everything at once.

cards.title: Three-to-four campaigns per week as your default cadence
cards.summary: Send 3–4 campaigns weekly to your engaged list to stay top of mind, provided the content is genuinely good.
cards.use_when: Setting your ongoing campaign frequency after recovery, or testing whether your current once-a-week rhythm is too thin.

cards.title: Text-based emails vs graphic emails A/B test
cards.summary: Test pure-text campaigns against graphic campaigns; the source's example showed text winning on clicks and placed orders.
cards.use_when: Planning a weekly A/B test, especially for a best-sellers or product roundup campaign where you'd default to heavy graphics.

cards.title: Judge subject-line tests on placed orders, not opens
cards.summary: Subject line can shift purchase behavior; measure its A/B test on placed order rate and revenue, not just open rate.
cards.use_when: Running subject-line tests on campaigns or abandonment emails, and deciding which subject line to roll out.

cards.title: Products vs categories in the email body
cards.summary: Test showing individual products against linking to category pages; higher-SKU brands may find individual products win.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to merchandise a campaign for a catalog with many SKUs — show specific products or send people to browse a category.

cards.title: Long-form vs short-form email body copy
cards.summary: Test longer founder-story copy against a few lines of text with a clear CTA; short won in the source's welcome-flow test.
cards.use_when: Writing a welcome-flow email or any campaign where you're tempted to explain product science, origin story or background at length.

cards.title: Test send time of day for campaigns
cards.summary: Morning vs late-afternoon sends can swing engagement sharply; dial in your brand's best window.
cards.use_when: After you've settled cadence and content, when tuning when campaigns actually go out.

cards.title: Test flow delay timing for site abandonment
cards.summary: A 30-minute reminder isn't always better than a 4-hour one — test delays in abandonment flows on placed order rate.
cards.use_when: Setting the delay on a browse/site abandonment flow or any reminder email where you've assumed 'strike while the iron is hot'.

cards.title: Branded text email vs plain native text email
cards.summary: Once you choose text-based sends, test a branded version (logo header/footer) against a fully plain native-format email.
cards.use_when: Executing text-based campaigns and deciding whether to include your logo and footer or send truly plain text.

cards.title: Weekly A/B test roster of high-leverage variables
cards.summary: Keep a standing list of high-leverage email variables and test one deliberately every week rather than tweaking two words monthly.
cards.use_when: Building a recurring experimentation plan for your email program so testing keeps producing revenue rather than becoming sporadic.

cards.title: Prime an LLM with brand context before writing email copy
cards.summary: Feed the model exhaustive brand, product, customer and voice information first so later copy prompts have real context.
cards.use_when: Setting up an AI-assisted email copy workflow for a store before generating any campaign copy.

cards.title: Prompt for graphic-email copy structure, then iterate
cards.summary: Ask for graphic-campaign copy with a punchy headline, subheadline and short body leading to a shop-now CTA, then refine across several rounds.
cards.use_when: Drafting hero and body copy for a graphic campaign and you want structured output instead of a wall of generic AI prose.

cards.title: Generate a year of non-discount email topics from micro-topics
cards.summary: Use a macro-to-micro prompt to produce broad themes and specific subtopics that become a full year of educational, non-discount campaigns.
cards.use_when: Planning a campaign calendar and running out of non-discount angles, especially for niche or technical product categories.

cards.title: Set SMS campaign frequency to 1–2 sends per week maximum
cards.summary: SMS hits the phone's primary app with a ding, so send far less often than email—one message per week as the default, occasionally two—to protect a hard-won list from unsubscribes.
cards.use_when: Deciding your monthly SMS campaign cadence and how many messages to schedule per week for your store's list.

cards.title: Budget SMS copy using the rendered segment count
cards.summary: Estimate actual message segments after personalization, links and required text rather than relying on a universal 160-character cutoff.
cards.use_when: Writing and editing SMS campaign or flow copy before sending, to control per-message cost.

cards.title: Check SMS encoding and segment cost before sending
cards.summary: Estimate actual message segments after personalization, links and required text rather than relying on a universal 160-character cutoff.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to include emojis in SMS campaign or flow copy to add visual interest without images.

cards.title: Reserve MMS images for campaigns where they earn 2–3x the SMS revenue
cards.summary: MMS (image) messages cost 2–3 times more than plain SMS, so include a picture only when the message can plausibly generate two to three times the revenue of a text-only send.
cards.use_when: Choosing between a plain-text SMS and an image MMS for a product launch or campaign send.

cards.title: Choose an SMS platform that consolidates with your existing email stack
cards.summary: Most SMS platforms do the same core things at similar prices, so pick one—ideally the same tool you already use for email—and ignore marginal AI feature comparisons.
cards.use_when: Selecting or switching an SMS provider for your store before building flows and campaigns.

cards.title: Grow the SMS list with a post-purchase opt-in checkbox
cards.summary: Add a marketing opt-in checkbox at checkout so every buyer passively contributes a phone number, giving you a growing list in the background.
cards.use_when: Setting up checkout and post-purchase list growth to continuously add SMS subscribers without extra traffic.

cards.title: Delay the SMS/email pop-up trigger to 6–10 seconds after page load
cards.summary: Trigger signup pop-ups on a 6–10 second time delay—not scroll or exit intent—to maximize views without hurting site conversions.
cards.use_when: Configuring the trigger and display rules of a website pop-up form that captures email and SMS subscribers.

cards.title: Build a two-step micro-commitment pop-up: email first, then phone
cards.summary: Ask for email in step one, then prompt for the phone number in step two with benefit-driven copy, which the source says converts roughly ten times better than asking for both at once.
cards.use_when: Designing the multi-step flow of a website signup pop-up to capture both email and SMS subscribers.

cards.title: Aim pop-up forms at 8–10% conversion vs the 2–3% baseline
cards.summary: Most audited brands convert only ~2–3% of visitors via pop-up; optimizing trigger, offer, and form simplicity can reach 8–10%, tripling list acquisition from same traffic.
cards.use_when: Benchmarking and improving the conversion rate of your site's email/SMS signup form against typical performance.

cards.title: Launch five core SMS automation flows before heavy campaign sending
cards.summary: Set up Welcome, Browse Abandonment, Cart Abandonment, Checkout Abandonment, and Win-back flows, keeping each short and high-ROI, since automations run in the background and earn clicks without extra effort.
cards.use_when: Building the automated SMS flow system for a store, or deciding which flows to prioritize first.

cards.title: Keep SMS campaigns transactional, urgent, or announcement-based—not nurture
cards.summary: SMS campaigns should carry product drops, special offers, restocks, and announcements; pure nurture or social-proof content tends to get high unsubscribes and poor ROI on SMS.
cards.use_when: Choosing what content types belong in the SMS campaign calendar versus what should stay in email.

cards.title: Model the SMS month around launches and flash sales, then fill the gaps
cards.summary: Anchor the SMS calendar on big events—product launches get 2–3 messages, flash sales get 2—then insert 2–3 filler campaigns (giveaway, restock) to keep a 1–2 per week cadence.
cards.use_when: Planning a store's monthly SMS campaign calendar around known launch and promotion dates.

cards.title: Test SMS send times; default to 11 a.m.–2 p.m. and 4–5 p.m.
cards.summary: There is no universal best send time, so test per audience; the source's safer windows are midday and early evening, avoiding pre-10 a.m. and post-7:30 p.m.
cards.use_when: Scheduling SMS campaigns and last-chance messages to maximize open and click response for your specific list.

cards.title: Treat the SMS list as a channel asset for revenue you control
cards.summary: The source frames SMS as a near-guaranteed-seen channel with very high open rates and an owned list—unlike ad accounts that platforms can shut down—and reports major contribution to store revenue.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest budget and team time in building an SMS channel versus relying solely on paid acquisition.

cards.title: Choose an SMS platform: consolidate with email, then price-shop
cards.summary: Pick SMS in the same platform as your email for management simplicity, but get competing quotes since SMS pricing varies and features rarely matter.
cards.use_when: Selecting or renegotiating the SMS/text platform for your store's lifecycle messaging.

cards.title: Capture phone numbers in your popup from day one
cards.summary: Add an SMS phone field to your email popup now, even with no SMS program, so your text list compounds instead of starting from zero later.
cards.use_when: Designing or revising the email/SMS signup popup that captures subscribers at store entry.

cards.title: Use a quiz popup and 'activate your discount' copy to lift phone capture
cards.summary: Lead with a micro-quiz before asking for contact info, and phrase the SMS ask as finishing the signup they already started.
cards.use_when: Building the SMS/phone opt-in step of your store popup to raise subscriber capture rate.

cards.title: Treat SMS as high-urgency, low-frequency — not a nurture channel
cards.summary: SMS tolerates far fewer sends than email; reserve it for time-sensitive, worth-the-ding messages or you get punishing unsubscribe rates.
cards.use_when: Deciding what content belongs in SMS blasts vs. email, and setting the tone of your text program.

cards.title: Budget SMS copy using the rendered segment count
cards.summary: Estimate actual message segments after personalization, links and required text rather than relying on a universal 160-character cutoff.
cards.use_when: Writing and budgeting SMS campaign and flow messages, especially for large lists.

cards.title: Test SMS vs. MMS images on net profit, not revenue
cards.summary: Image (MMS) messages can lift revenue and buyer intent but cost ~3x, so decide by net profit after send cost, not top-line revenue.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to include product images in SMS campaigns or abandonment flows.

cards.title: Build the five core SMS flows (welcome + four abandonments + post-purchase)
cards.summary: Every brand should run a welcome flow, site/browse/cart/checkout abandonment, and a post-purchase replenishment or win-back flow.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing the automated (flow) side of an SMS program.

cards.title: Structure the SMS welcome flow: day 1, day 3, day 5
cards.summary: Send a tight three-message SMS welcome — intro with discount, educational reminder, then last-chance — inside a short window while subscribers are warm.
cards.use_when: Writing the SMS welcome series triggered by your popup signup.

cards.title: Send only one SMS per abandonment event (US compliance)
cards.summary: US rules limit abandonment flows to a single SMS per recipient within 48 hours, so keep cart/browse/checkout texts to one simple message.
cards.use_when: Setting up SMS cart, browse, site, or checkout abandonment flows, especially for US customers.

cards.title: Time post-purchase and replenishment SMS to the buy cycle
cards.summary: Send a cross-sell/upsell SMS about 10–14 days after delivery and a replenishment reminder just before the product runs out.
cards.use_when: Building the post-purchase and replenishment SMS flow for your store.

cards.title: Trigger SMS win-back at double the average time between purchases
cards.summary: Use 2x the customer's average reorder interval as the win-back trigger, then send a short 72-hour flash offer plus a last-chance reminder.
cards.use_when: Setting the trigger point and offer structure for an SMS win-back flow for lapsed buyers.

cards.title: Cap SMS blasts at about two campaigns per week for most brands
cards.summary: Baseline around two SMS campaigns weekly, reserving higher frequency for launch-heavy or aggressive-acquisition brands with big lists.
cards.use_when: Setting the SMS campaign (blast) calendar and frequency for your store.

cards.title: Plan an SMS campaign calendar around high-urgency events
cards.summary: Fill the SMS calendar with launches, restocks, time-boxed sales and timely trend/drop alerts — not evergreen nurture.
cards.use_when: Building the monthly SMS campaign calendar and choosing which messages to send.

cards.title: Broadcast SMS to the full list with a tight exclusion list
cards.summary: Default to sending SMS to all subscribers and only suppress chronically unengaged numbers, cleaning monthly — deep engagement segmentation leaves money on the table.
cards.use_when: Segmenting your SMS list for campaign sends and deciding send exclusions.

cards.title: Test delays, offers and images before scaling SMS
cards.summary: Validate timing, offer and image choices with A/B tests and your own brand context rather than copying a template wholesale.
cards.use_when: Deciding what to change or expand once your core SMS flows and campaigns are running.

cards.title: Three components of a converting email: copy, structure, design
cards.summary: Break every ecommerce email into copywriting, structure and graphic design, then evaluate each separately against the goal of driving a purchase click.
cards.use_when: Planning a campaign or flow email (promo, launch, replenishment reminder) and deciding where a weak performer is failing before redesigning it.

cards.title: 'Button at the top' rule for non-scrollers
cards.summary: Place the logo, headline, short copy and a large primary CTA fully above the fold so non-scrolling readers still have a path to purchase.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing the hero section of any promotional or lifecycle email where you need clicks from subscribers who never scroll.

cards.title: Email structure: hero, bridge, repeated CTAs, footer navigation
cards.summary: Use a repeating structure — hero pitch with button, informational bridge with an infographic, benefit/product section with another button, then category-navigation footer.
cards.use_when: Building or templating a promotional email layout, or fixing an email where traffic stops partway down the page.

cards.title: Make the email scroll feel seamless with gradients and flowing backgrounds
cards.summary: Use continuous background colors and gradients between sections so readers don't notice section breaks and keep scrolling into lower CTAs.
cards.use_when: Designing a long image-based email where readers drop off at section boundaries, or matching section backgrounds in Figma.

cards.title: Skimmable copy: pain headline, one-sentence body, three selling points
cards.summary: Write email copy for a three-second skim: call out the customer's pain in the headline, keep the largest block to one sentence, and sell on no more than three points.
cards.use_when: Writing or editing the copy for a promo, launch or replenishment email, especially when the current draft is paragraph-heavy.

cards.title: Reverse-engineer competitor emails into a reusable copy template with ChatGPT
cards.summary: Feed a competitor email to ChatGPT, have it extract the structural template, then have it write new copy for your brand using that exact formula.
cards.use_when: You need fast email copy drafts and have identified competitor emails whose structure and angle perform well in your category.

cards.title: Build emails as stacked image slices, not one giant image
cards.summary: Design the email in Figma, slice it into separate images for links and load speed, then stack them in the ESP.
cards.use_when: Producing an image-based email design and preparing assets for upload into Klaviyo, Omnisend or a similar ESP.

cards.title: Hidden footer text to protect text-to-image deliverability ratio
cards.summary: Append a block of invisible body text at the bottom of image-heavy emails so spam filters see a healthy text-to-image ratio.
cards.use_when: Sending an email built mostly or entirely from images, where the HTML contains very little real text.

cards.title: Laying out an email design in Figma without advanced tools
cards.summary: Map the email as labelled placeholder blocks in a Figma frame first, then replace them with brand assets, so the layout is decided before detail work.
cards.use_when: Starting a new email design from scratch and you need to establish section order before choosing images and colours.

cards.title: Us-versus-them comparison block built with icon checkmarks
cards.summary: Create an explicit comparison graphic with checkmarks for your brand and X marks for competitors to make the product's advantages unmissable before the closing CTA.
cards.use_when: Writing the bridge or product-proof section of an email where the differentiator needs to be stated clearly (e.g., ingredient quality, sourcing, process).

cards.title: Put footer navigation to work for non-buyers
cards.summary: Use the footer to offer category, quiz and social links so readers who scrolled past the featured product still have somewhere to click.
cards.use_when: Designing the bottom of a promotional email where the featured product may not match every reader.

cards.title: Upload a finished image-design email into an ESP as stacked images
cards.summary: Set up a campaign, strip the template, upload compressed slices in order, remove padding, add links, then test and send.
cards.use_when: Publishing an image-based email built in Figma into Omnisend, Klaviyo or a similar platform.

cards.title: Image-only vs text-and-HTML emails: the presenter's position
cards.summary: The presenter argues image-only emails are standard practice among large brands and text/HTML is not required in 2026; treat this as a contested practice with real trade-offs.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to build an email as stacked images or as HTML text with styled blocks.

cards.title: Compress and slice images to protect load time in the inbox
cards.summary: Keep individual email slices small and compress them before upload, because a single full-email image slows loading in the customer's inbox.
cards.use_when: Exporting a long designed email from Figma and preparing the files for ESP upload.

cards.title: Design principles that keep emails converting and subscribers subscribed
cards.summary: Use big buttons, matched accent colours, infographics and careful small details to make emails engaging without relying on flashy effects.
cards.use_when: Finishing or reviewing an email design before upload, especially when the layout works but feels flat or off-brand.

cards.title: Use conversational messaging to resolve product-purchase friction
cards.summary: When shoppers need help with product fit, compatibility or a cart decision.
cards.use_when: When shoppers need help with product fit, compatibility or a cart decision.

cards.title: Reduce signup fields while retaining clear messaging consent
cards.summary: When simplifying a store text-message signup form.
cards.use_when: When simplifying a store text-message signup form.

cards.title: Test concise conversational welcome messages
cards.summary: When welcoming a shopper who opted into the store messaging program.
cards.use_when: When welcoming a shopper who opted into the store messaging program.

cards.title: Hand product questions to a trained human
cards.summary: When a messaging flow receives replies requiring individualized help.
cards.use_when: When a messaging flow receives replies requiring individualized help.

cards.title: Use short product demos to answer a shopper question
cards.summary: When a opted-in conversation needs a clearer product explanation than text.
cards.use_when: When a opted-in conversation needs a clearer product explanation than text.

cards.title: Measure conversational messaging by purchases and support outcomes
cards.summary: When evaluating store messaging flows or comparing supported channels.
cards.use_when: When evaluating store messaging flows or comparing supported channels.

cards.title: Email System Build Order: List Growth → Flows → Campaigns → Tests → Deliverability → AI
cards.summary: Build the email program in dependency order, starting with signup forms, because each layer's performance depends on the layer below it.
cards.use_when: Planning an email marketing roadmap or auditing why email revenue is flat before buying new tactics or tools.

cards.title: Signup Form Offer Design and Margin Math
cards.summary: Pick the opt-in incentive by testing offer types against signup rate, welcome-flow conversion and attributed revenue, not signup rate alone.
cards.use_when: Choosing or refreshing the incentive on the popup, full-page or embedded opt-in form on the store.

cards.title: Standard Popup Structure: One Headline, One Field, One CTA, One Microcopy
cards.summary: Keep the opt-in form to four elements and remove every block that does not move the visitor toward the email field.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing the layout of a desktop popup opt-in or full-page signup form.

cards.title: Micro-Commitment (Micro-Yes) Step Before the Email Field
cards.summary: Insert a one-question yes/no step before the email field to create commitment, then measure whether it lifts total signups for your audience.
cards.use_when: Optimizing the opt-in form flow on a popup to raise email capture rate.

cards.title: Timing, Frequency and Device Targeting Rules for Popups
cards.summary: Test popup timing, repeat exposure and device-specific targeting to balance signups with the shopping experience.
cards.use_when: Configuring when and how often the opt-in popup fires on the storefront, generally or per device.

cards.title: Teaser / Floating Button Configuration
cards.summary: Keep a persistent teaser or floating button so visitors who close the popup still have a visible path back to the offer.
cards.use_when: Adding or reviewing the teaser (Klaviyo) or floating button (Aliyah/Shopify app) that accompanies the opt-in popup.

cards.title: Post-Opt-In Success Page: Withhold the Code, Train Email Opens
cards.summary: Route new subscribers to their inbox for the discount instead of displaying it on the success page, to protect first-email engagement signals.
cards.use_when: Writing the success/confirmation screen copy that appears after a visitor submits their email on the opt-in form.

cards.title: Separate Desktop and Mobile Signup Forms
cards.summary: Clone the desktop form into a dedicated mobile form and fix the specific elements that break at small sizes.
cards.use_when: Adapting an existing opt-in popup for mobile traffic, or before starting device-level A/B tests.

cards.title: Redirect Your Signup Offer Away From Cart and Checkout Traffic
cards.summary: Suppress discount popups for visitors in the cart and checkout so you do not discount orders that would have completed at full price.
cards.use_when: Configuring URL inclusion and exclusion rules for the opt-in popup on an ecommerce store.

cards.title: Compress Signup Form Images to Protect Load Time
cards.summary: Run every image used in an opt-in form through compression before uploading, because load time is a major conversion killer.
cards.use_when: Preparing product or lifestyle imagery for a signup popup, full-page form or landing page opt-in.

cards.title: Ten Common Signup Form Mistakes to Audit Against
cards.summary: Audit a live opt-in form against the source's recurring failure modes, led by a weak offer.
cards.use_when: Reviewing an underperforming opt-in form or onboarding a store's existing email capture setup.
